description_full: Avio S.p.A. designs, develops, produces, and integrates space launchers in Italy and internationally. The company involved in the design, development, and production of solid and liquid propulsion systems for launchers; design, development, and production of solid propulsion systems for tactical missiles; development, integration, and supply of complete light space launchers; research and development of new environmentally friendly propulsion systems and attitude control engines for satellites; liquid propulsion systems for satellites; and ground infrastructure for launcher preparation and launch. Avio S.p.A. was founded in 1984 and is headquartered in Colleferro, Italy.

financial_summary: AVIO SPA is a mid-cap industrials business with a $2.1B market cap on $638M of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +19% over the past three years, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder.
Returns on capital run at 2% against a 9% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests. Gross margins of 71% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $136M in free cash flow — roughly 21 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 16.04× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage of 27× is fortress-like.

Net dilution runs at 20.1% annually, transferring value from owners to stock-based comp, and insiders hold 28% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and profit capture is only 0.1× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.

Cyclicality and capital intensity — order books turn on a dime, and the heavy fixed cost base that creates the moat also magnifies the downturn.
Supply chain reshoring costs and labour shortages — onshoring mandates raise capex requirements while a shrinking skilled-labour pool inflates operating costs.
Tariff and trade-policy exposure — industrial exporters sit squarely in the crosshairs of protectionist policy, and retaliatory tariffs can close markets without warning.

sect: Its 2% operating margin trails the Industrials median (9%) by 8pp, so it is a below-average operator in its field.
It captures well under its share of sector profits (0.14x its revenue share).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.01 across 550 companies in the universe; the top four hold 9% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 21% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 15% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 71% and a beta of 0.96, it moves roughly with the market.
Trading is thin (about $19K a day), below the $1.0M liquidity floor flagged; building a position would move the price.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $26.17 (margin of safety -62%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 58%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $14.35 to $58.27 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
Multiples send mixed signals against Industrials peers: cheaper on P/FCF 15.3 vs 22.4, richer on P/E 75.9 vs 23.1 and EV/EBITDA 61.4 vs 13.3 (sector median).
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 6.5% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 0.7% (vs the 8% bar).
The price implies 17.0% annual cash-flow growth, 11pp more than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 2% falls short of the cost of capital of 9.3%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.33).
It runs a 71% gross margin and converts 21% of revenue into free cash flow.
ROE of 2% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.4x equity multiplier).
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $308.2M.
Warning signs: an Altman Z of 1.80 in the distress zone.
The value-trap profile is elevated (54/100); see the breakdown below.
The Beneish M-score (-2.13) sits just under the manipulation line, so earnings quality bears watching.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 19.0% over 3 years.
At current returns, reinvesting 100% of profits supports about 2.2% a year of fundamental growth, too little to drive meaningful growth.
own: Insiders own 27.8%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 44%.
Net share issuance leaves shareholder yield negative (-20.1%), diluting holders.
people: With about 1,643 employees, each generates about $389K of revenue, in line with the Industrials median.
That works out to $83K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $922K (2x revenue per employee).
